module_1_v1.video_title: What is Investing? Basics for Beginners

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of investing?
options: Growing wealth by putting money to work
questions.concept: Investing means allocating money with the expectation of generating a return, allowing wealth to grow beyond simple savings.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an asset class?
questions.concept: Stocks, bonds, real estate, and gold are asset classes. A grocery bill is a consumption expense, not an investment.

questions.q: What is the relationship between risk and return in investing?
options: Higher risk always means lower returns
Higher risk usually means potential for higher returns
Lower risk always means higher returns
questions.concept: The risk-return tradeoff is fundamental: to earn higher potential returns, an investor must accept higher risk.

questions.q: Which Indian regulator oversees the stock market?
questions.concept: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) regulates and supervises Indian capital markets, protecting investor interests.

questions.q: What does 'capital appreciation' mean?
options: Interest earned from a savings account
An increase in investment value over time
questions.concept: Capital appreciation is the rise in the market price of an asset above the price paid for it.

questions.q: How does inflation affect money kept idle in cash?
questions.concept: Inflation erodes purchasing power. ₹1,000 today will buy less in the future if kept idle, making investing important.

questions.q: What is a key benefit of starting to invest early?
options: Taking advantage of compound interest over a longer period
questions.concept: Starting early maximises compounding — earnings generate their own earnings over time, creating exponential growth.

questions.q: What is a 'portfolio' in investing?
options: A collection of financial investments held by an individual
questions.concept: A portfolio is the entire set of investments held by an investor — stocks, mutual funds, bonds, gold, and real estate.

questions.q: Which of the following is considered a liquid investment?
questions.concept: Listed stocks can be sold on any trading day, making them highly liquid compared to real estate or locked FDs.

questions.q: What is the key difference between saving and investing?
options: Saving stores money safely; investing puts money to work for growth
questions.concept: Saving preserves money for future use; investing deploys capital with the goal of growth, accepting some level of risk.

module_1_v2.video_title: How to Open a Demat Account in India

questions.q: What does 'Demat' stand for?
questions.concept: Demat stands for Dematerialised — holding securities in electronic form rather than physical paper certificates.

questions.q: Which two depositories operate Demat accounts in India?
questions.concept: NSDL (National Securities Depository Limited) and CDSL (Central Depository Services Limited) are India's two depositories.

questions.q: What is a Depository Participant (DP)?
options: An intermediary (like a broker) that opens and manages Demat accounts
questions.concept: A DP is an agent of the depository — typically a bank or broker — through which investors open and operate Demat accounts.

questions.q: Which document is mandatory for KYC when opening a Demat account?
questions.concept: PAN is mandatory for all financial transactions in India. Aadhaar is used for identity and address verification during KYC.

questions.q: What is the annual maintenance charge (AMC) for a Demat account?
options: A yearly fee charged by the DP for maintaining the Demat account
questions.concept: AMC is an annual fee charged by the DP to maintain your Demat account, covering administrative and operational costs.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of holding shares in Demat form?
options: Eliminates risks of theft, loss, or forgery of paper certificates
questions.concept: Demat eliminates problems with physical shares: loss, theft, damage, fake certificates, and lengthy transfer processes.

questions.q: Can you have multiple Demat accounts in India?
options: Yes, but only with the same broker
Yes, you can open multiple accounts with different DPs
questions.concept: An investor can open multiple Demat accounts with different DPs. Each must maintain proper KYC.

questions.q: What is a Trading Account and how does it differ from a Demat Account?
options: Trading account executes buy/sell orders; Demat account holds securities
Demat is for trading; Trading holds shares
questions.concept: A Trading Account places orders on exchanges. A Demat Account is an electronic vault where purchased securities are stored.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT required to open a Demat account?
questions.concept: Essentials for Demat account: PAN, Aadhaar/address proof, bank account details, and a photograph. Property docs are not needed.

questions.q: After buying shares, under T+1 settlement, when are shares credited to your Demat?
questions.concept: India operates on T+1 settlement — shares are credited to your Demat account within 1 trading day after the transaction.

module_1_v3.video_title: Share Market Basics for Beginners in Hindi

questions.q: What is a stock exchange?
options: A marketplace where buyers and sellers trade stocks and securities
questions.concept: A stock exchange is an organised marketplace where buyers and sellers trade financial instruments like stocks, bonds, and derivatives.

questions.q: What does BSE stand for?
questions.concept: BSE stands for Bombay Stock Exchange, established in 1875 — Asia's oldest stock exchange.

questions.q: What is the SENSEX?
options: An index tracking 30 large-cap BSE-listed companies
The total value of all stocks in India
questions.concept: SENSEX (Sensitive Index) is BSE's benchmark tracking the performance of the top 30 well-established companies.

questions.q: What does NIFTY 50 represent?
options: The top 50 large-cap companies listed on NSE
questions.concept: NIFTY 50 is NSE's benchmark index, representing the weighted average of 50 of India's largest companies across sectors.

questions.q: What happens when you buy a share of a company?
options: You lend money to the company
You become a partial owner of the company
questions.concept: Buying a share makes you a shareholder — a partial owner. Your wealth grows as the company grows.

questions.q: What is a bull market?
options: A market where prices are falling
A market where prices are rising with investor optimism
A market for agricultural commodities only
questions.concept: A bull market is characterised by rising stock prices (typically 20%+ from recent lows) and widespread optimism.

questions.q: What is market capitalisation?
options: Total value of a company's outstanding shares (share price × total shares)
questions.concept: Market cap = Current share price × Total number of outstanding shares. It measures the total market value of a listed company.

questions.q: Which regulator sets rules for stock exchanges in India?
questions.concept: SEBI regulates and develops the securities market in India, protecting investor interests and ensuring fair practices.

questions.q: What is an IPO?
options: Initial Public Offering — when a company first lists on a stock exchange
questions.concept: An IPO (Initial Public Offering) is when a private company offers shares to the public for the first time, listing on a stock exchange.

questions.q: What does 'circuit breaker' mean in stock markets?
options: A physical switch in trading terminals
A mechanism that halts trading when prices move too sharply up or down
questions.concept: Circuit breakers automatically halt trading temporarily when a stock or index moves beyond a pre-set percentage limit.

module_1_v4.video_title: Stock Market for Beginners — Full Playlist Intro

questions.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary market?
options: Primary: IPOs/new issues; Secondary: trading existing shares between investors
Primary for large investors; Secondary for retail
Primary for bonds; Secondary for stocks
questions.concept: In the primary market, companies raise fresh capital via IPOs. In the secondary market, investors buy and sell existing securities among themselves.

questions.q: What is the face value of a share?
options: Original nominal value stated in the company's charter
questions.concept: Face value (par value) is the original nominal value of a share — common values in India are ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, or ₹10.

questions.q: What are equity shares?
options: Ownership units giving holders voting rights and share in profits
questions.concept: Equity shares represent ownership in a company. Equity shareholders have voting rights, receive dividends, and benefit from capital appreciation.

questions.q: What is a 'bear market'?
options: A sustained decline in prices (generally 20%+ from recent high)
A market dominated by bear traders
A market open only at night
questions.concept: A bear market is a prolonged fall in stock prices, typically 20% or more from recent highs, accompanied by widespread pessimism.

questions.q: What is a dividend?
options: A share of profits distributed by a company to its shareholders
A penalty for selling shares early
questions.concept: A dividend is a portion of a company's profits distributed to shareholders as a reward for holding the stock.

questions.q: What is intraday trading?
options: Holding stocks for more than a year
Buying and selling the same stock within the same trading day
questions.concept: Intraday trading involves buying and selling the same stock within one trading session (9:15 AM–3:30 PM). Positions must close before market end.

questions.q: What is a stock broker?
options: A SEBI-registered intermediary who executes buy/sell orders on behalf of investors
questions.concept: A stockbroker is a SEBI-registered intermediary who executes securities transactions on behalf of investors on NSE and BSE.

questions.q: What is 'delivery' in stock trading?
options: Buying shares and holding them in Demat beyond the trading day
questions.concept: Delivery trading means buying shares and holding them in your Demat account overnight or longer for medium/long-term investing.

questions.q: What is upper/lower circuit on a stock?
options: Maximum and minimum price a stock can move in a single trading day
questions.concept: Upper circuit is the maximum price a stock can rise (e.g., 5%, 10%, 20%) in a day; lower circuit is the maximum it can fall. Trading halts at these limits.

questions.q: What does 'shorting' a stock mean?
options: Buying a small quantity of a stock
Selling a stock you don't own, hoping to buy it back cheaper later
Holding a stock for a short period
questions.concept: Short selling means selling borrowed shares expecting the price to fall, then buying back at a lower price to profit from the difference.

module_1_v5.video_title: How to Buy Your First Stock — Step by Step

questions.q: What is the correct sequence to buy your first stock?
options: Open Demat+Trading → Fund account → Research → Place order
questions.concept: Correct process: 1) Open Demat+Trading, 2) Complete KYC, 3) Add funds, 4) Research stocks, 5) Place a buy order.

questions.q: What is a 'limit order'?
options: An order to buy/sell at the exact price you specify
An order that executes at any market price
An order that never gets executed
An order placed by a broker automatically
questions.concept: A limit order specifies the exact price you want. It only executes when the market reaches your price, giving you price control.

questions.q: What is a 'market order'?
options: An order placed at a specific price
An order that buys/sells at the current best available market price immediately
A bulk order only for institutions
questions.concept: A market order executes immediately at the best available price. It guarantees execution but not the exact price.

questions.q: What is brokerage?
options: A fee charged by the broker for executing your trades
questions.concept: Brokerage is the commission charged by a stockbroker for facilitating your buy/sell transactions.

questions.q: What taxes apply when you sell stocks held for less than 12 months?
options: No tax if profit is below ₹1 lakh
questions.concept: Profits from stocks held for less than 12 months are taxed as STCG at 20% (revised in Budget 2024).

questions.q: What is Securities Transaction Tax (STT)?
options: A tax levied on every buy/sell transaction of listed securities
A fee paid to stock exchanges
questions.concept: STT is a transaction tax collected by the government on every purchase and sale of listed securities, deducted automatically at trade.

questions.q: What does 'average down' mean?
options: Selling a stock when it goes down
Buying more shares at a lower price to reduce your average cost per share
Setting a stop loss below current price
questions.concept: Averaging down means purchasing more shares when the price falls, reducing your overall average cost per share.

questions.q: What should you do BEFORE buying any stock?
options: Research the company's fundamentals, financials, and business model
Wait for it to be on the news
Buy whatever is trending on social media
questions.concept: Proper research is essential: understand the company's business, financial health, management quality, valuation, and competitive position.

questions.q: What is a 'stop-loss order'?
options: An order to buy more when a stock falls
An order that automatically sells when it falls to a specified price, limiting losses
An order only placed by institutions
questions.concept: A stop-loss automatically triggers a sell order when a stock's price drops to a specified level, protecting you from larger losses.

questions.q: Which best describes fundamental analysis?
options: Evaluating a company's financial health and business quality to determine true value
questions.concept: Fundamental analysis studies a company's financials (P&L, balance sheet, cash flows), business model, management, and industry to assess intrinsic value.

module_1_v6.video_title: Investing with Just ₹1,000 — Where to Start

questions.q: What minimum amount can you start investing in stocks?
options: As low as ₹1 (price of one share)
questions.concept: You can start investing with as little as the price of one share. Some mutual funds allow ₹100–₹500 via SIP.

questions.q: What allows you to start investing with ₹500/month in a mutual fund?
questions.concept: SIP allows investing a fixed small amount (as low as ₹100–₹500) every month in a mutual fund.

questions.q: With ₹1,000, which is the most diversified starting option?
options: Buying one share of a single company
Investing in an index mutual fund or ETF
questions.concept: An index fund/ETF tracking NIFTY 50 gives instant diversification across 50 companies with just ₹1,000.

questions.q: What is the key advantage of starting small vs waiting to accumulate more?
options: You earn better returns by waiting
Starting small gives time in the market, allowing compounding from day one
Brokers offer better rates for small investments
questions.concept: Time in the market beats timing the market. Small amounts invested early benefit from compound growth over years.

questions.q: Which is a good first investment for a beginner with ₹1,000?
questions.concept: Large-cap index funds are the best start: diversified, low expense ratios, tracks established companies, and requires minimal research.

questions.q: What is an ETF (Exchange Traded Fund)?
options: A fund that tracks an index and trades like a stock on the exchange
A fixed deposit with high returns
questions.concept: An ETF is a basket of securities (like stocks in an index) that trades on a stock exchange like a single stock.

questions.q: Why is diversification important even with small amounts?
options: It is not important for small investors
It spreads risk so a loss in one investment doesn't wipe out everything
questions.concept: Diversification reduces unsystematic risk. Poor performance of one investment is offset by others in a diversified portfolio.

questions.q: What is 'cost averaging' with regular small investments?
options: Buying more units when prices are low and fewer when high by investing fixed amounts regularly
questions.concept: Cost averaging means investing a fixed amount regularly — you buy more units when prices are low and fewer when high, reducing average cost.

questions.q: Which is safer with ₹1,000: one stock or a diversified fund?
options: One stock for higher potential return
A diversified fund because risk is spread across many assets
Neither is safe — only keep cash
questions.concept: A diversified fund spreads your ₹1,000 across many companies automatically, dramatically reducing single-stock risk.

questions.q: What should be your FIRST financial priority before investing?
options: Build an emergency fund of 3–6 months of expenses
questions.concept: Build an emergency fund covering 3–6 months of living expenses before investing, preventing forced liquidation during crises.

questions.q: What is the PRIMARY function of a Demat account?
questions.concept: A Demat account acts as an electronic vault holding your purchased securities in dematerialised form after trades settle.

questions.q: What is the PRIMARY function of a Trading account?
options: Executing buy and sell orders on stock exchanges
questions.concept: A Trading account is the interface connecting you to stock exchanges. You place buy/sell orders; shares then move to/from Demat.

questions.q: Can you have a Demat account without a Trading account?
options: Yes — you can hold securities in Demat but need a Trading account to transact
Trading account is not required in India
questions.concept: Yes — you can hold a Demat independently for shares received as gifts or ESOPs, but need a Trading account to actively buy/sell.

questions.q: Which entities operate Demat accounts in India?
questions.concept: NSDL and CDSL are the two depositories. They operate through Depository Participants (banks, brokers, financial institutions).

questions.q: What is a 'DP ID'?
options: A unique identifier for the Depository Participant
questions.concept: DP ID is the unique identifier for your Depository Participant. Combined with your client ID, it forms your Demat account number.

questions.q: What is a 3-in-1 account?
options: Possible through banks linking savings, trading, and Demat together
questions.concept: Several banks (HDFC, ICICI, Kotak) offer 3-in-1 accounts linking a savings account, trading account, and Demat account seamlessly.

questions.q: What happens to shares if your broker shuts down?
options: Shares remain safe — held by NSDL/CDSL, not the broker
questions.concept: Shares are held by the depository (NSDL/CDSL), not by the broker. Even if a broker fails, your shares remain safe.

questions.q: What does 'BOID' mean?
options: Beneficiary Owner Identification number — your unique Demat account identifier
questions.concept: BOID (Beneficiary Owner Identification) is your unique 16-digit Demat account number, essential for receiving shares and corporate actions.

questions.q: What is the role of CDSL's 'Easiest' facility?
options: Allowing investors to authorize transfer instructions online without a physical DIS slip
questions.concept: CDSL's Easiest is an internet-based facility that electronically authorises debit instructions, eliminating physical DIS slips.

questions.q: What charges are associated with a Demat account?
options: AMC (annual maintenance), transaction fees, and dematerialisation charges
questions.concept: Demat accounts may involve: AMC (annual fee), transaction charges (per debit instruction), and dematerialisation/rematerialisation charges.

module_1_v8.video_title: What are Stocks, Shares, Equity — Simply Explained

questions.q: What is the difference between 'stocks' and 'shares'?
options: Stocks refers to ownership broadly; shares refers to specific units of one company
Stocks for companies; shares for mutual funds
questions.concept: Stocks is a general term for ownership in corporations. Shares are individual units of a particular company's stock. Often used interchangeably.

questions.q: What gives equity shareholders a say in company decisions?
options: Voting rights attached to equity shares
Being a customer of the company
questions.concept: Equity shareholders have voting rights — typically one vote per share — allowing participation in key decisions like electing the board.

questions.q: What is 'EPS' (Earnings Per Share)?
options: Net profit divided by number of outstanding shares
questions.concept: EPS = Net Profit ÷ Total Outstanding Shares. It shows how much profit each share earns, helping compare profitability across companies.

questions.q: What is a bonus share?
options: Additional free shares issued to existing shareholders proportionally
Shares given as an employee benefit
questions.concept: Bonus shares are free additional shares given to existing shareholders in a set ratio (e.g., 1:1). Share price adjusts proportionally; total value stays same.

questions.q: What is a stock split?
options: Dividing existing shares into multiple shares to improve liquidity and affordability
questions.concept: A stock split divides existing shares (e.g., 2:1 split = each share becomes 2). Price halves, market cap stays same, making shares more affordable.

questions.q: What are preference shares?
options: Shares with preferential rights to dividends and assets, typically without voting rights
questions.concept: Preference shareholders receive fixed dividends before equity shareholders and have priority in asset distribution during liquidation.

questions.q: What is 'book value' per share?
options: Net assets divided by total outstanding shares
Price at which shares were first issued
Maximum price a share can reach
questions.concept: Book value per share = (Total Assets − Total Liabilities) ÷ Outstanding Shares. It represents the theoretical net asset value per share.

questions.q: What is 'Return on Equity' (ROE)?
options: Net profit divided by shareholders' equity — measures how efficiently a company uses shareholder funds
questions.concept: ROE = Net Profit ÷ Shareholders' Equity × 100. Higher ROE indicates a company generates more profit per rupee of equity.

questions.q: What does 'promoter holding' indicate?
options: Percentage of shares held by the company's founders/promoters
questions.concept: Promoter holding is the % of shares held by founders/promoters. High promoter holding signals confidence; pledging of promoter shares is a red flag.

questions.q: What is a rights issue?
options: A legal right to sue a company
An offer to existing shareholders to buy additional shares at a discounted price
New shares sold only to foreign investors
questions.concept: A rights issue lets existing shareholders buy additional shares at a discounted price before the offer is made to the general public.

module_1_v9.video_title: Common Beginner Mistakes in the Stock Market

questions.q: What is one of the most common beginner mistakes in investing?
options: Following social media tips and buying without research
questions.concept: Acting on unverified tips from social media or WhatsApp without independent research is one of the biggest and most costly beginner mistakes.

questions.q: What is 'FOMO' in investing?
options: Fear Of Missing Out — buying assets because they are rising, not based on fundamentals
questions.concept: FOMO leads investors to chase rising stocks at high valuations, often entering near the top and suffering significant losses when the trend reverses.

questions.q: Why is trying to 'time the market' considered a mistake?
options: It is an excellent strategy for all investors
It is impossible to consistently predict market tops and bottoms; time in the market beats timing
It only works for large investors
questions.concept: Consistently predicting market peaks and troughs is extremely difficult even for professionals. Staying invested long-term outperforms frequent in-out strategies.

questions.q: What does 'putting all eggs in one basket' mean in investing?
options: Concentrating all investments in one stock — high risk if it fails
questions.concept: Concentration risk: if you invest everything in one stock and it collapses, you lose everything. Diversification across sectors mitigates this.

questions.q: What is the mistake of 'panic selling'?
options: Selling investments in fear during a downturn, often at the worst prices
questions.concept: Panic selling during corrections locks in losses permanently. Markets recover over time, so selling in panic often destroys long-term wealth.

questions.q: What is 'overtrading' and why is it harmful?
options: Investing in too many mutual funds
Buying and selling too frequently, resulting in high brokerage/tax costs that erode returns
questions.concept: Overtrading increases transaction costs (brokerage, STT, taxes) and is emotion-driven. It consistently underperforms a simple buy-and-hold approach.

questions.q: What is 'anchoring bias' in investing?
options: Fixating on a past price (e.g., what you paid) rather than evaluating current fundamentals
questions.concept: Anchoring bias: being mentally 'anchored' to a reference price (your purchase price) leads to poor decisions like refusing to sell a bad stock.

questions.q: Why should beginners avoid F&O (Futures & Options)?
options: F&O involves high leverage, complexity, and time decay — most beginners lose money
F&O is not available in India
F&O has lower taxes than equity
questions.concept: SEBI data shows 90%+ of individual F&O traders lose money. Derivatives require deep understanding of leverage, Greeks, and time decay.

questions.q: What is a 'hot tip' and why should you be cautious?
options: An unverified investment recommendation that could be based on rumor or manipulation
A tip from a certified financial advisor
questions.concept: Hot tips are often part of 'pump and dump' schemes where promoters inflate prices via rumors, then sell, leaving retail investors with losses.

questions.q: What is the importance of reviewing your portfolio periodically?
options: Portfolios should never be reviewed once set up
Regular review ensures alignment with goals and allows rebalancing when needed
Reviews are only needed during market crashes
questions.concept: Periodic portfolio review (annually or semi-annually) ensures investments align with your financial goals, risk tolerance, and time horizon.

module_1_v10.video_title: SEBI and Investor Protection in India

questions.q: When was SEBI established?
questions.concept: SEBI was established in 1992 under the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992. It replaced the Controller of Capital Issues (CCI).

questions.q: What is SEBI's primary mandate?
options: Protecting investor interests and regulating the securities market
Setting repo and reverse repo rates
questions.concept: SEBI's three key functions: protecting investor interests, developing the securities market, and regulating market intermediaries.

questions.q: What is the SCORES portal?
options: SEBI's online complaint redressal system for investors
questions.concept: SCORES (SEBI Complaints Redress System) is an online platform where investors can lodge complaints against listed companies, brokers, and other registered entities.

questions.q: What is 'insider trading'?
options: Trading from inside a broker's office
Trading using material non-public information about a company — illegal in India
questions.concept: Insider trading means buying/selling securities based on material, non-public information. It's illegal under SEBI regulations and carries heavy penalties.

questions.q: What is the IEPF?
options: A government fund for stock market losses
A fund holding unclaimed dividends and matured deposits, managed by the government
questions.concept: IEPF holds unpaid dividends unclaimed for 7+ years. Investors can claim their dues from IEPF even after years of non-collection.

questions.q: What is 'front running' in stock markets?
options: A broker trading on their own account ahead of a large client order to profit from price movement
The opening trade of the day
questions.concept: Front running is illegal: a broker trades in their own account before executing a large client order, exploiting advance knowledge of the coming price movement.

questions.q: What is the maximum investor compensation if a SEBI-registered broker defaults?
options: Through Investor Protection Fund (IPF) up to ₹25 lakh
questions.concept: NSE and BSE have Investor Protection Funds (IPF) that compensate investors if their registered broker defaults — maximum ₹25 lakh per investor.

questions.q: What does 'due diligence' mean before investing?
options: Thorough research and verification of an investment opportunity before committing money
questions.concept: Due diligence means thoroughly investigating a company's financials, management, business model, and risks before investing.

questions.q: What should you do if you receive an unsolicited stock tip promising guaranteed returns?
options: Ignore or report to SEBI — guaranteed returns are a red flag for fraud
Invest a small amount to test
questions.concept: Guaranteed returns in equity markets signal fraud. SEBI regularly warns investors about unregistered advisors promising unrealistic returns.

questions.q: What is a 'Qualified Institutional Buyer' (QIB)?
options: SEBI-recognised institutions like mutual funds, banks, and FIIs eligible for certain offerings
questions.concept: QIBs are institutional investors (mutual funds, insurance companies, FPIs, banks) presumed to have expertise to evaluate investment risks.

questions.q: What is goal-based investing?
options: Aligning investments with specific financial goals and timelines
questions.concept: Goal-based investing means identifying specific financial goals, estimating required corpus, timeline, and working backwards to determine how much to invest.

questions.q: Why is a timeline important for a financial goal?
options: It determines investment risk level — longer timeline allows more equity, shorter requires more stability
questions.concept: Longer timelines allow higher equity allocation since volatility smooths out over time. Shorter timelines need stable instruments to protect capital.

questions.q: What is an 'inflation-adjusted goal'?
options: A goal that accounts for the rising cost of what you're saving for in the future
questions.concept: If you need ₹10 lakh today for a car, you might need ₹14-15 lakh in 5 years due to inflation. Inflation-adjusting your goal prevents a shortfall.

questions.q: What is 'goal segmentation'?
options: Splitting your investment into random parts
Categorising financial goals into short-term (0-3yr), medium-term (3-7yr), and long-term (7yr+)
questions.concept: Segmenting goals by timeline allows matching each goal with appropriate investment instruments — liquid funds for short-term, equity for long-term.

questions.q: What is the first step in goal-based investing?
options: Clearly define each financial goal, amount needed, and timeline
questions.concept: The foundation of goal-based investing is defining goals precisely — retirement at 60 needing ₹5 crore, child education in 15 years needing ₹50 lakh, etc.

questions.q: Which instrument is best for a 1-year goal (e.g., vacation fund)?
options: Liquid mutual fund or short-term FD
questions.concept: For 1-year goals, capital preservation matters most. Liquid funds or short-term FDs protect principal while earning modest returns with full liquidity.

questions.q: What is 'reverse goal planning'?
options: Working backwards from your target corpus to determine monthly investment needed today
questions.concept: Reverse planning: define target (e.g., ₹1 crore in 20 years), assume returns (12%), and calculate required monthly SIP — the goal drives the investment plan.

questions.q: What is a 'financial goal tracker'?
options: A tool or spreadsheet tracking progress toward each financial goal over time
A type of mutual fund statement
questions.concept: A goal tracker monitors whether your investments are on pace to meet each goal, allowing timely adjustments if you're falling behind or ahead.

questions.q: What happens if you don't define a goal before investing?
options: You may invest in wrong instruments, withdraw at wrong times, and fail to meet financial needs
questions.concept: Without goals, investors often panic-sell during crashes, chase hot sectors, or withdraw funds prematurely — destroying the wealth-building process.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a well-defined financial goal?
options: 'I need ₹20 lakh for my child's college education in 12 years'
'I'll start investing when markets are right'
questions.concept: A well-defined goal is SMART: Specific (₹20 lakh), Measurable, Achievable, Relevant (education), and Time-bound (12 years).

module_3_v2.video_title: How to Plan for a Car / House / Wedding

questions.q: What is a home loan EMI?
options: Equated Monthly Installment — fixed monthly payment covering principal and interest
questions.concept: EMI = Equated Monthly Installment. It's the fixed amount paid monthly to repay a loan, comprising principal repayment and interest.

questions.q: What is the ideal EMI-to-income ratio for a home loan?
options: Not more than 35-40% of monthly income
questions.concept: Financial advisors recommend keeping total EMIs (all loans) below 35-40% of monthly income to maintain financial stability and emergency flexibility.

questions.q: What is a down payment for a house?
options: The upfront amount paid when purchasing a property (typically 20% of property value)
questions.concept: Banks typically finance up to 80% of property value. The remaining 20% (or more) must be paid upfront as the down payment by the buyer.

questions.q: What is 'pre-payment' of a home loan?
options: Paying extra amounts toward the loan principal to reduce outstanding debt and save interest
questions.concept: Pre-payment reduces outstanding principal, significantly lowering total interest paid over the loan tenure and potentially reducing tenure itself.

questions.q: What is a car loan's typical tenure in India?
questions.concept: Car loans in India typically have tenures of 1-7 years, with 5 years being most common. Shorter tenure means higher EMI but lower total interest paid.

questions.q: Why is buying a depreciating asset like a car on loan risky?
options: The car's value falls while you pay interest — you pay more than the car is worth
questions.concept: Cars depreciate 15-20% per year. A car bought for ₹10 lakh may be worth ₹5 lakh in 5 years, but you've paid ₹12+ lakh (loan + interest).

questions.q: What is a 'balloon payment' loan structure?
options: Smaller monthly EMIs throughout the tenure with a large final payment at the end
A loan for salaried employees only
questions.concept: Balloon payment loans have lower EMIs but require a large lump sum at the end. This can be dangerous if not planned for — ensure you'll have the funds.

questions.q: What does CIBIL score have to do with loans?
options: A credit score (300-900) that determines loan eligibility and interest rate — higher is better
questions.concept: CIBIL score (credit score) reflects your creditworthiness. A score above 750 typically gets you lower interest rates and faster loan approvals.

questions.q: What is the best strategy for planning a major purchase like a house?
options: Save for down payment first, calculate EMI affordability, maintain emergency fund, then purchase
questions.concept: Planned major purchases: save down payment (20%+), ensure EMIs are within 35-40% of income, keep emergency fund intact, then proceed.

questions.q: What is 'opportunity cost' of buying a home vs renting and investing?
options: No difference between buying and renting
Down payment + EMIs invested in equity might generate higher returns than property appreciation in many Indian cities
questions.concept: In many Indian cities, rental yield is only 2-3% while equity markets return 12%+. The down payment invested in equity may outperform property appreciation — the buy-vs-rent calculation is nuanced.

module_3_v3.video_title: Financial Planning for 20s and 30s in India

questions.q: What are the key financial priorities in your 20s?
options: Building an emergency fund, starting SIP, getting term insurance, and staying debt-free
questions.concept: Your 20s are the most powerful investing decade — compounding works longest. Key priorities: emergency fund, term insurance, SIP in equity, avoid lifestyle debt.

questions.q: What financial moves are critical in your 30s?
options: Increase SIP amounts, buy health insurance, consider home loan if financially ready, review portfolio
questions.concept: In your 30s: step up SIPs with salary hikes, secure health coverage for family, plan for children's education, and review whether goals are on track.

questions.q: What is 'lifestyle inflation' and why is it dangerous?
options: Spending more as you earn more, leaving no surplus for investment goals
questions.concept: Lifestyle inflation means each salary hike is consumed by upgraded lifestyle (bigger car, eating out more), preventing wealth accumulation despite higher income.

questions.q: What is 'human capital' in personal finance?
options: Your future earning capacity — the present value of all future income from your career
questions.concept: Human capital is your most valuable asset in your 20s — investing in skills, education, and career development maximises future income and investing capacity.

questions.q: Why should young investors take more equity risk?
options: Longer time horizon means more time to recover from market downturns; compounding maximises with equity returns
questions.concept: With a 30-40 year investment horizon, short-term market volatility becomes irrelevant. Equity's higher returns over long periods create dramatically more wealth than conservative investments.

questions.q: What is a 'term insurance' and why is it essential in your 20s-30s?
options: An investment that returns money at term end
Pure life insurance giving high coverage for low premium — essential to protect dependents if you die early
questions.concept: Term insurance provides ₹1-2 crore coverage for ₹500-1000/month premium. It's pure protection — if you die during the term, your family gets the sum assured. Essential when you have dependents.

questions.q: What is the '50-30-20 rule' of budgeting?
questions.concept: 50-30-20 budget rule: allocate 50% of income to essential needs (rent, food, EMIs), 30% to discretionary wants, and 20% to savings and investments.

questions.q: What financial goal is most critical to plan in your 30s?
options: Children's education and retirement — both are large, long-horizon goals that need early planning
questions.concept: Children's education (15-18 year horizon) and retirement (25-30 year horizon) require the earliest possible planning. Delaying even 5 years dramatically increases required monthly investment.

questions.q: What does 'net worth' mean in personal finance?
options: Total assets minus total liabilities — the true measure of financial health
questions.concept: Net Worth = Total Assets (savings, investments, property, gold) − Total Liabilities (loans, credit card debt). Tracking net worth annually shows your true financial progress.

questions.q: What is 'sinking fund' in personal financial planning?
options: A dedicated savings pool for known future expenses (e.g., car purchase, vacation, home renovation)
questions.concept: A sinking fund is money set aside regularly for planned future expenses. Instead of taking a loan when you need ₹1 lakh for a car repair, your sinking fund covers it.

module_4_v1.video_title: Risk Profiling — Are You Aggressive or Conservative

questions.q: What is 'risk profiling'?
options: Assessing your ability and willingness to take financial risk based on income, goals, and psychology
questions.concept: Risk profiling identifies your risk capacity (financial ability to absorb losses) and risk appetite (psychological comfort with volatility) to design an appropriate investment portfolio.

questions.q: What are the three main risk profiles?
questions.concept: Conservative investors prioritize capital protection; moderate investors balance growth and safety; aggressive investors maximise growth potential accepting high volatility.

questions.q: Which portfolio allocation suits an aggressive investor?
questions.concept: Aggressive investors (typically young, high income, long horizon) can allocate 80-100% to equity, accepting short-term volatility for maximum long-term compounding.

questions.q: What factors determine an investor's risk capacity?
options: Income stability, emergency fund, debt levels, time horizon, and financial responsibilities
questions.concept: Risk capacity = financial ability to absorb losses. It depends on stable income, adequate emergency fund, low debt, long investment horizon, and few dependents.

questions.q: What is the difference between risk appetite and risk capacity?
options: Risk appetite = psychological willingness to accept risk; Risk capacity = financial ability to sustain losses
questions.concept: You may have a high risk appetite (want high returns) but low risk capacity (single income, EMIs, dependents). Investing at higher risk than capacity is dangerous.

questions.q: A 55-year-old near retirement should have what type of asset allocation?
options: More conservative — shift toward debt/bonds to protect accumulated corpus
questions.concept: Near retirement, capital preservation outweighs growth. Shifting to conservative instruments (debt funds, bonds) protects against a major market crash wiping out retirement savings.

questions.q: What is 'loss aversion' in investing psychology?
options: The tendency to avoid all investments
The psychological tendency to feel the pain of losses about twice as intensely as the pleasure of equivalent gains
questions.concept: Loss aversion (Kahneman & Tversky) means a ₹1 lakh loss feels twice as painful as a ₹1 lakh gain feels pleasurable. This leads to poor decisions like panic selling.

questions.q: What is the 'age rule' for equity allocation?
options: 100 minus your age = equity %; rest in debt (e.g., age 30 → 70% equity)
Invest 50% in equity at all ages
questions.concept: The 100-age rule is a simple heuristic. At 30: 70% equity, 30% debt. At 50: 50% equity, 50% debt. Some use 110 or 120 instead of 100 for today's longer lifespans.

questions.q: What is a risk questionnaire used for?
options: Assessing risk profile through questions about goals, income, reaction to loss, and time horizon
A SEBI compliance requirement for brokers
questions.concept: Risk questionnaires help identify your risk profile through standardised questions about income stability, investment goals, time horizon, and emotional reaction to portfolio losses.

questions.q: What is the most important factor in determining your investment style?
options: Your own risk profile, goals, time horizon, and financial situation — unique to every investor
The most popular investment of the year
questions.concept: Investment style must be personalised — there's no universal 'best' portfolio. Your risk capacity, time horizon, goals, and emotional temperament define the right allocation for you.

questions.q: What is 'active investing'?
options: Selecting specific stocks/funds attempting to outperform the market through research and analysis
questions.concept: Active investing involves selecting individual stocks or actively-managed funds with the goal of beating benchmark index returns through in-depth research.

questions.q: What is 'passive investing'?
options: Investing in index funds that replicate a market index without trying to beat it
Letting a fund manager decide everything
questions.concept: Passive investing replicates a market index (like NIFTY 50) without active stock selection. The goal is to match, not beat, market returns at minimal cost.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of passive/index investing?
options: Higher returns than active funds always
Lower expense ratios, no manager bias, and data shows most active funds underperform their index long-term
questions.concept: Index funds have expense ratios as low as 0.1% vs 1-2% for active funds. Studies show 80-90% of active funds underperform their benchmark index over 10+ years.

questions.q: What is an 'expense ratio' and why does it matter in passive vs active comparison?
options: Annual fee % charged by a fund house; lower expense ratio = more returns for investor
questions.concept: Expense ratio is the annual management fee. A 1.5% active fund vs 0.1% index fund on ₹10 lakh over 20 years = difference of ₹3+ lakh in final corpus due to compounding of fees.

questions.q: What is 'tracking error' in an index fund?
options: The deviation between the index fund's returns and the actual index returns — lower is better
questions.concept: Tracking error measures how closely an index fund replicates its benchmark. Lower tracking error = better replication. This is a key metric when comparing index funds.

questions.q: Can active fund managers consistently beat the market?
options: Research (SPIVA report) shows fewer than 20-30% of active funds consistently outperform their benchmark over 10+ year periods
questions.concept: The SPIVA (S&P Indices Versus Active) report shows 70-80% of actively managed funds in India underperform their benchmark index over 10 years after fees — a powerful argument for passive investing.

questions.q: What is the 'core and satellite' portfolio strategy?
options: Core: 70-80% in stable index funds; Satellite: 20-30% in high-conviction active bets for outperformance
questions.concept: Core-satellite combines stability and opportunity: the core (index funds) provides reliable market returns while the satellite (active picks) offers potential alpha on a manageable portion.

questions.q: Which is more tax-efficient between active and passive investing?
options: Passive index funds are generally more tax-efficient due to lower turnover (fewer transactions triggering capital gains)
questions.concept: Active funds frequently buy and sell securities (high turnover), generating taxable capital gains events within the fund. Index funds have minimal turnover, reducing internal tax drag.

questions.q: In which market condition does active investing have a potential advantage?
options: In inefficient or less-analysed market segments (e.g., small-cap, mid-cap, emerging markets) where information gaps exist
questions.concept: Active management may add value in inefficient markets (small-cap, sector-specific) where thorough research can identify genuinely mispriced securities. In highly efficient large-cap markets, it's harder to add alpha.

questions.q: If you are a first-time investor with limited time to research, which is more suitable?
options: A passive index fund tracking NIFTY 50 — zero research needed, market returns, low cost
questions.concept: First-time investors should start with passive index funds: no stock-picking required, automatic diversification, low cost, and returns match the Indian economy's growth over time.

module_5_v1.video_title: Asset Allocation — The Most Important Decision

questions.q: What is 'asset allocation'?
options: Dividing money between different bank accounts
Distributing investments across asset classes (equity, debt, gold) based on goals and risk profile
questions.concept: Asset allocation is the foundational portfolio construction decision — how to divide your investment across equity, debt, gold, real estate, and cash based on your risk profile and goals.

questions.q: Why is asset allocation considered more important than stock selection?
options: Research shows 90%+ of long-term portfolio returns are determined by asset allocation, not individual stock/fund selection
questions.concept: The Brinson, Hood, Beebower study found ~91% of portfolio return variation is explained by asset allocation decisions, not stock/fund selection or market timing.

questions.q: What is the typical equity-debt-gold split for a moderate risk investor?
questions.concept: A moderate risk investor (30-45 age range) often uses 50-60% equity for growth, 30-40% debt for stability, and 10% gold as an inflation hedge and crisis protector.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'debt' in a portfolio?
options: To provide stability, regular income, and reduce portfolio volatility during equity market crashes
Debt is never useful in a portfolio
questions.concept: Debt instruments (bonds, debt mutual funds, FDs) provide stability and act as a shock absorber when equity markets fall, ensuring you have liquid funds without selling equities at a loss.

questions.q: Why include gold in a portfolio?
options: Gold has a low/negative correlation with equities — when stocks crash, gold often rises, providing portfolio protection
questions.concept: Gold's negative correlation with equities makes it an excellent portfolio diversifier. During financial crises (2008, 2020), gold rose while equities crashed, protecting portfolio value.

questions.q: What is 'rebalancing' a portfolio?
options: Selling all investments and starting fresh
Periodically adjusting portfolio back to target allocation after market movements have shifted percentages
questions.concept: Rebalancing restores target allocation. If equity rises from 60% to 75% of portfolio, you sell some equity and buy debt/gold to return to 60-30-10 — systematically 'selling high, buying low'.

questions.q: What is correlation in portfolio construction?
options: A statistical relationship between returns of two assets — lower correlation = better diversification
The return relationship between your income and investments
questions.concept: Correlation measures how two assets move relative to each other. Assets with low or negative correlation (e.g., equity and gold) provide better diversification — one's loss is partially offset by the other's gain.

questions.q: What is 'systematic rebalancing' vs opportunistic rebalancing?
options: Systematic: rebalance on a fixed schedule (annually); Opportunistic: rebalance when allocation drifts beyond a threshold (e.g., ±5%)
Opportunistic only works for large portfolios
questions.concept: Annual systematic rebalancing is simple and avoids over-trading. Threshold-based rebalancing (e.g., when equity drifts ±5% from target) is more responsive but creates more taxable events.

questions.q: What is 'strategic vs tactical asset allocation'?
options: Strategic: long-term target allocation; Tactical: short-term deviations based on market views
Strategic is better for all investors
Tactical is the only valid approach
questions.concept: Strategic allocation sets your long-term target (e.g., 60:30:10). Tactical allocation allows temporary deviations based on market opportunities (e.g., increasing equity during a crash).

questions.q: What is the 'rebalancing benefit' in volatile markets?
options: Rebalancing forces you to buy assets that have fallen (underweighted) and sell those that have risen (overweighted) — disciplined contrarian action
It is only for conservative investors
questions.concept: Rebalancing enforces discipline: when markets crash, equity falls below target, so you buy more equity (at low prices). When markets rally, you sell equity (at high prices) to restore balance.

module_6_v1.video_title: What Happens if the Market Crashes 50%

questions.q: What typically happens during a stock market crash?
options: All stocks go to zero permanently
Stock prices fall sharply due to panic, economic fears, or systemic risks — but historically recover over time
questions.concept: Market crashes are sharp price declines (20%+ from peaks) driven by panic, recession fears, or systemic events. Every historical crash — 1929, 2000, 2008, 2020 — has been followed by recovery.

questions.q: What should a long-term investor do during a market crash?
options: Stay invested or buy more at lower prices — don't panic; crashes are opportunities for long-term investors
Take all money out and put in savings account
questions.concept: Long-term investors should view crashes as sales — quality assets at discounted prices. Historical data shows investors who stayed invested through every crash recovered and ultimately prospered.

questions.q: What is a 'circuit breaker' at the market level (not stock level)?
options: A power outage in the exchange
An automatic halt in ALL market trading when NIFTY falls more than a set percentage in a day (SEBI-mandated)
questions.concept: Market-wide circuit breakers halt all trading for 15-45 minutes when NIFTY falls 10%, 15%, or 20% in a day — giving time for the panic to subside and preventing complete market collapse.

questions.q: What is a 'flight to safety' during market crashes?
options: Investors moving money from risky assets (equities) to safe haven assets (gold, government bonds, FDs)
questions.concept: During crashes, investors sell equities and move to safe assets — government bonds, gold, and FDs — driving their prices up while equity markets fall further.

questions.q: What is the most psychologically difficult part of investing in a crash?
options: Staying invested when your portfolio is down 40%+ and news is extremely negative — resisting panic selling
questions.concept: Human psychology makes holding during crashes extremely difficult. Loss aversion, fear, and doom-and-gloom media create immense pressure to sell exactly when staying invested is most important.

questions.q: What is 'dollar-cost averaging' during a crash?
options: Continuing or increasing regular investments during a crash to buy more units at lower prices
questions.concept: Continuing SIP during a crash means buying more units at lower prices. When markets recover, these cheaper units generate amplified returns — the silver lining of market downturns.

questions.q: What is 'margin of safety' as an investing concept during volatile times?
options: Buying assets significantly below their intrinsic value to provide protection if your analysis is wrong
questions.concept: Margin of safety (Benjamin Graham's concept) means only buying when an asset trades well below intrinsic value. In crashes, many quality assets offer this margin, making them compelling investments.

questions.q: What does 'this too shall pass' mean in market crash context?
options: Historical evidence shows all market crashes, no matter how severe, eventually recover — patience is rewarded
questions.concept: Every major crash — Great Depression, 2008 Financial Crisis, COVID 2020 — was followed by recovery and new highs. This historical pattern is the strongest argument for staying invested.

questions.q: What is 'bear market rally'?
options: A temporary price rise within an ongoing bear market that can mislead investors into thinking the crash is over
questions.concept: Bear market rallies are sharp, short-term bounces within a longer downtrend. Inexperienced investors may think recovery has begun and buy in, only to see prices fall further.

questions.q: What is the most important thing to have in place BEFORE a market crash hits?
options: A solid financial plan: emergency fund, diversified portfolio, clear goals, and psychological preparedness to not panic
questions.concept: Financial resilience before a crash is critical: an emergency fund prevents forced selling, diversification limits damage, clear goals remind you why you're invested, and mental preparedness prevents panic.

questions.q: What does RBI's 'repo rate' represent?
options: Rate at which banks lend to customers
Rate at which RBI lends money to commercial banks — affects all interest rates in the economy
questions.concept: Repo rate is the rate at which RBI provides short-term funds to commercial banks. When RBI raises repo rate, borrowing costs rise across the economy, typically impacting equities negatively.

questions.q: How does an RBI rate hike typically affect stock markets?
options: Markets often fall — higher rates increase borrowing costs for companies, reduce growth prospects, and make fixed income more attractive
questions.concept: Rate hikes are generally negative for equities: higher borrowing costs compress corporate margins, reduce consumer spending, and make bonds more attractive relative to stocks.

questions.q: What does 'monetary policy' mean?
options: RBI's management of money supply and interest rates to achieve economic objectives (inflation control, growth)
questions.concept: Monetary policy involves RBI controlling the money supply and interest rates through tools like repo rate, CRR, and SLR to balance inflation control with economic growth.

questions.q: What is the 'Monetary Policy Committee' (MPC)?
options: A 6-member RBI committee that decides interest rate changes every 6-8 weeks — decisions significantly move markets
questions.concept: The MPC meets every 6-8 weeks to vote on repo rate changes. Their decisions — hike, cut, or hold — are major market-moving events that investors closely watch.

questions.q: What is 'CRR' (Cash Reserve Ratio)?
options: The minimum percentage of deposits that banks must keep with RBI — used to control money supply
questions.concept: CRR is the portion of bank deposits that must be held with RBI. Higher CRR reduces money available for lending, contracting money supply and vice versa.

questions.q: What does 'hawkish' monetary policy mean?
options: A stance favouring higher interest rates to control inflation — markets often react negatively
questions.concept: Hawkish = inflation-fighting focus, favouring rate hikes. Dovish = growth focus, favouring rate cuts. RBI's hawkish or dovish stance significantly guides market expectations.

questions.q: How does a rate cut typically affect equity markets?
options: Markets often rally — cheaper credit boosts corporate profits, consumer spending, and makes equities more attractive vs lower-yielding bonds
questions.concept: Rate cuts lower borrowing costs for companies (better margins) and consumers (more spending). They also make fixed income less attractive, pushing investors toward equities — typically bullish for markets.

questions.q: What is 'yield curve inversion' and why does it matter?
options: When short-term bond yields exceed long-term yields — historically a reliable recession predictor
questions.concept: A normal yield curve has higher long-term yields. When it inverts (short > long), it signals market expectations of future rate cuts and economic slowdown — historically precedes recessions by 6-18 months.

questions.q: What is 'GDP growth rate' and its impact on stock markets?
options: The pace of economic expansion — higher GDP growth generally supports corporate earnings and equity market returns
questions.concept: GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth reflects economic health. Higher GDP growth leads to better corporate revenues and earnings, supporting equity market returns. India's 6-8% GDP growth supports strong equity markets.

questions.q: What is the significance of 'global cues' for Indian markets?
options: Global factors (US Fed decisions, China data, oil prices) significantly influence Indian market sentiment and FPI flows
questions.concept: Indian markets are increasingly integrated with global markets. US Fed rate changes, China's economy, crude oil prices, and global risk sentiment all significantly impact Indian equity and currency markets.

module_8_v1.video_title: Technical Analysis for Beginners — Full Guide

questions.q: What is technical analysis?
options: Studying price charts and trading patterns to predict future price movements based on historical data
questions.concept: Technical analysis uses historical price and volume data to identify patterns, trends, and signals that suggest future price direction — without considering company fundamentals.

questions.q: What is a 'candlestick chart'?
options: A bar chart for company revenues
A financial chart showing open, high, low, and close prices for each time period in a candle-like visual format
A type of mutual fund performance chart
questions.concept: A candlestick displays 4 price points: Open, High, Low, Close. Green/white candles = price rose; Red/black candles = price fell. Patterns in candlesticks signal potential reversals or continuations.

questions.q: What is 'support' in technical analysis?
options: A price level where demand is strong enough to prevent further price decline — stocks tend to 'bounce' off support
questions.concept: Support is a price floor where buying interest overcomes selling pressure. When a stock repeatedly holds above a price level, that level is considered 'support'.

questions.q: What is 'resistance' in technical analysis?
options: A price level where selling pressure prevents further price increase — stocks tend to stall or reverse at resistance
questions.concept: Resistance is a price ceiling where selling overcomes buying. A stock that repeatedly fails to break above a price level has 'resistance' at that level. Breaking above resistance is a bullish signal.

questions.q: What is a 'moving average'?
options: The average daily movement of the SENSEX
An average of prices over a specified period that smooths out short-term volatility to show the underlying trend
questions.concept: A moving average (e.g., 50-day or 200-day) averages closing prices over the period. It smooths noise and shows the underlying trend direction. Prices above the MA suggest uptrend.

questions.q: What does it mean when a stock's price crosses above its 200-day moving average?
options: A bullish signal suggesting the stock may be shifting from downtrend to uptrend
questions.concept: The 200-day MA is a key long-term trend indicator. When price crosses above it (after being below), it signals potential trend reversal from bearish to bullish — often watched closely by traders.

questions.q: What is 'volume' in trading and why does it matter?
options: The number of shares traded in a period — high volume on a price move confirms the move's strength; low volume suggests it's weak
The total value of a company
questions.concept: Volume validates price movements. A price breakout with high volume = strong confirmation. A price move on low volume = less reliable, more likely to reverse.

questions.q: What is the 'Relative Strength Index' (RSI)?
options: A comparison of one stock vs another
A momentum indicator (0-100 scale) measuring speed and magnitude of price changes — above 70 = overbought, below 30 = oversold
questions.concept: RSI oscillates between 0-100. RSI > 70 suggests a stock is overbought (potential pullback). RSI < 30 suggests oversold (potential bounce). It helps identify extreme conditions.

questions.q: What is a 'breakout' in technical analysis?
options: When price moves decisively above a resistance level or below a support level, often signaling a new trend direction
A type of mutual fund strategy
questions.concept: A breakout occurs when price surpasses a key level (resistance or support) with significant volume. Breakouts above resistance signal potential bullish momentum; breakdowns below support signal bearish momentum.

questions.q: What is the P/E ratio in fundamental analysis?
options: Price to Earnings — current share price divided by EPS; indicates how much investors pay per rupee of earnings
questions.concept: P/E = Price ÷ EPS. A P/E of 20 means you pay ₹20 for every ₹1 of earnings. Lower P/E vs peers may indicate undervaluation; higher P/E suggests either growth expectations or overvaluation.

questions.q: What caused the 2008 global financial crisis?
options: Collapse of the US subprime mortgage market, causing a global banking system crisis that spread worldwide
questions.concept: The 2008 crisis originated from US subprime mortgage defaults, which had been packaged into complex financial derivatives (CDOs/MBS) held by banks globally — when mortgages failed, banks collapsed.

questions.q: How did Indian markets react during the 2008 financial crisis?
options: SENSEX fell ~60% from its 2008 peak, but recovered to new highs by 2010-2014, rewarding patient investors
Indian markets rose during the crisis
questions.concept: India's markets fell ~60% during the 2008 crisis despite India's banking system being relatively sound. But the crash was followed by strong recovery — NIFTY 50 reached new all-time highs by 2010.

questions.q: What is 'systemic risk'?
options: Risk of a single company failing
Risk that the failure of one entity can cascade through the entire financial system — interconnected risk
A type of mutual fund risk
questions.concept: Systemic risk is the collapse risk of an entire financial system, not just individual parts. Lehman Brothers' failure in 2008 created systemic risk as its counterparties also faced crisis.

questions.q: What is a 'contagion' in financial markets?
options: The spread of financial crisis from one market/country/institution to others through financial linkages and panic
questions.concept: Financial contagion occurs when a crisis in one sector or country rapidly spreads to others through investor panic, credit linkages, and cross-border exposures.

questions.q: What is 'moral hazard' in financial regulation?
options: When entities take excessive risks knowing they'll be bailed out if things go wrong — banks in 2008 engaged in this behavior
questions.concept: Moral hazard occurs when protection from consequences encourages riskier behavior. Pre-2008, banks took excessive risks believing governments would bail them out — proven true in 2008.

questions.q: What key lesson did the 2008 crisis teach individual investors?
options: Leverage amplifies both gains and losses; diversification is critical; and no asset class is immune to systemic risk
questions.concept: 2008 showed: highly leveraged positions can be catastrophic; seemingly safe assets (AAA-rated CDOs) can become worthless; global diversification provides imperfect protection; cash is king in a crisis.

questions.q: What is a 'credit default swap' (CDS)?
options: A financial derivative that allows one party to transfer credit risk of a bond to another — widely blamed for amplifying the 2008 crisis
questions.concept: CDS are insurance-like contracts on bond defaults. In 2008, huge CDS exposures on subprime mortgages meant defaults cascaded — institutions that had 'insured' these bonds couldn't pay claims.

questions.q: How can studying historical crises help investors?
options: Understanding past crises reveals patterns: overleverage, speculation bubbles, contagion — helping investors avoid similar mistakes and maintain perspective during future crashes
Historical crises are irrelevant to India
questions.concept: History rhymes: bubbles in tulips (1637), railways (1840s), dot-com (2000), real estate (2008) share common themes of excess leverage, speculation, and eventual collapse. Pattern recognition prevents emotional mistakes.

questions.q: What is 'deleveraging' in the context of financial crises?
options: The process of reducing debt levels — forced deleveraging (selling assets to repay loans) during crises drives asset prices down further
questions.concept: Forced deleveraging: when markets fall and lenders demand loan repayments, borrowers sell assets regardless of price, causing further price drops, causing more margin calls — a self-reinforcing downward spiral.

questions.q: What is the 'Lehman moment' concept?
options: The catastrophic turning point in a crisis where a major institution's failure triggers system-wide panic — referencing Lehman Brothers' 2008 collapse
questions.concept: Lehman Brothers' September 2008 bankruptcy was the 'point of no return' in the crisis — too big to save but too big to fail. It froze global credit markets and triggered the worst financial panic since 1929.

module_tax_v1.video_title: STCG vs LTCG on Stocks and Mutual Funds

questions.q: What is STCG (Short Term Capital Gains) on equity in India?
options: Gains from selling equity held less than 12 months — taxed at 20%
questions.concept: STCG on listed equity (sold within 12 months) is taxed at 20% (revised from 15% in Budget 2024). This applies to all equity and equity mutual funds.

questions.q: What is LTCG (Long Term Capital Gains) on equity in India?
options: No tax if held over 1 year
Gains from equity held more than 12 months — taxed at 12.5% on gains exceeding ₹1.25 lakh per year
questions.concept: LTCG on listed equity (held 12+ months) is taxed at 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh per year (revised in Budget 2024 from ₹1 lakh exemption at 10%).

questions.q: What is 'tax harvesting' in equity investing?
options: Strategically selling investments at a loss to offset capital gains, reducing tax liability
questions.concept: Tax loss harvesting: intentionally selling loss-making investments to book losses that offset gains, reducing your net capital gains tax. The sold assets can be repurchased after a brief period.

questions.q: Which mutual fund category qualifies for 80C tax deduction?
options: ELSS (Equity Linked Savings Scheme) — 3-year lock-in with up to ₹1.5 lakh deduction per year
questions.concept: ELSS provides dual benefit: potential equity returns + tax deduction up to ₹1.5 lakh under Section 80C. It has the shortest lock-in (3 years) among all 80C instruments.

questions.q: What is STT (Securities Transaction Tax)?
options: A transaction tax collected at source on every buy/sell of listed securities — already deducted by broker
questions.concept: STT is a small percentage levied on every stock/equity mutual fund transaction. It's deducted automatically by the broker/exchange and cannot be set off against capital gains.

questions.q: How are F&O (Futures & Options) profits taxed?
options: As business income (not capital gains) — taxed at your applicable income tax slab rate
questions.concept: F&O income is treated as business/speculative income, taxed at your income slab rate (up to 30%). This is why F&O trading requires proper accounting and ITR-3 filing.

questions.q: What is the benefit of the 'Growth option' over 'Dividend option' for mutual funds from a tax perspective?
options: Growth option defers taxation until redemption — dividends are taxed as income in the year received at slab rate, creating an immediate tax liability
Growth option is taxed every year
questions.concept: Growth option: gains are taxed only at redemption (as LTCG/STCG). Dividend option: dividends are added to income and taxed at your slab rate when declared — creating regular tax drag that erodes compounding.

questions.q: What is ITR-2 primarily used for?
options: For individuals with income from capital gains (stocks, mutual funds, property) who are not running a business
questions.concept: ITR-2 is for individuals and HUFs with income from salary, house property, capital gains (stocks, MF, property), and other sources — but not business/professional income.

questions.q: What is 'grandfathering' in the context of LTCG tax on equity (introduced in 2018)?
options: Equity gains accumulated before January 31, 2018 are not taxed — only gains from Feb 1, 2018 onwards are taxable as LTCG
A type of tax exemption scheme
questions.concept: When LTCG tax was reintroduced in 2018, the government 'grandfathered' all gains on equity till Jan 31, 2018. The cost basis for LTCG calculation is the higher of actual purchase price or Jan 31, 2018 price.

questions.q: What is the tax treatment of debt mutual fund gains (as of FY2024)?
options: LTCG at 10% if held over 3 years
Regardless of holding period, debt fund gains are taxed as per income slab rate (no indexation benefit since April 2023)
questions.concept: From April 2023, debt mutual fund gains are taxed at income slab rates regardless of holding period — the previous 20% with indexation benefit was removed, making FDs and debt funds tax-equivalent.
